title: Paragraph Completion — Tone-Matching
tagline: Year 3 — Choosing the closing sentence that fits the logic, direction and tone of the paragraph

introduction.overview: A paragraph-completion question gives a paragraph without its final sentence and asks you to choose the sentence that finishes it best. The right sentence continues the direction of the argument (support, contrast or result), keeps the tone (formal, ironic, sad, cautious), stays in scope, and neither repeats nor leaps ahead. Wrong options typically fail on one of these four.
introduction.placementRelevance: Paragraph-completion items appear in verbal sections along with para jumbles and sentence completion.
introduction.realWorldContext: Ending an email, a report or a paragraph in the right voice uses the same judgement.

learningObjectives: Identify the direction: support, contrast or result
Choose balanced endings for balanced paragraphs
Prefer the option that closes the thought

prerequisiteKnowledge.quickRefresher: The last sentence of a paragraph usually gives the result, the conclusion or the next step.

coreDefinitions: Direction: whether the paragraph is supporting, contrasting or concluding.
Tone: the attitude of the paragraph (formal, ironic, regretful, cautious, persuasive).
Scope: the topic limits of the paragraph.
Repetition: restating an earlier sentence without adding anything.
Leap: jumping to a new topic or an extreme claim.
conceptExplanation.theoreticalIntuition: Read the paragraph as a sentence that has not finished yet. The ending should feel like the only natural way to stop.
conceptExplanation.visualOrMentalModel: Name the direction and tone in two words ("sad, result"; "balanced, conclusion"). Keep only options that match both, then discard repeats and leaps.

mainNarrative: Take a paragraph that praises a restaurant: "The restaurant had received glowing reviews for its food. Critics praised the fresh ingredients, the generous portions and the friendly staff." The direction is a result of the praise: "It is no surprise that the tables are booked weeks in advance." An option about the building being constructed in 1950 leaves the topic.

For a balanced paragraph ("Critics say the policy will raise prices. Supporters say it will protect local jobs."), a balanced ending fits: "Both claims may be partly true, so the answer depends on how the policy is designed." An option that declares the policy harmful picks a side that the paragraph has not taken.
A formal letter needs a formal close: "We thank you for your interest and wish you every success in the future." A casual or boastful ending would clash with the register.

In an ironic paragraph, the ending should extend the irony: after a slogan promising "service with a smile" and forty minutes on hold, the line about the recorded voice thanking him for his patience carries the joke further.
A suspense paragraph needs a suspenseful ending: "Somewhere below, a door creaked slowly open." A calm summary would break the mood.

deepDiveAspects.title: Hedged endings
deepDiveAspects.content: In scientific paragraphs, an ending that asks for more evidence matches a paragraph that reports early results.

deepDiveAspects.title: The restatement trap
deepDiveAspects.content: An option that merely repeats the previous sentence is wrong even if it matches the tone.

solvedExamples.title: Result
solvedExamples.question: A paragraph says critics praised a restaurant's fresh food and friendly staff. Which ending fits: "It is no surprise that its tables are booked weeks ahead" or "The building was constructed in 1950"?

steps.title: Choice
steps.explanation: Advance booking follows from praise; the building is off-topic.

solvedExamples.finalAnswer: It is no surprise that its tables are booked weeks ahead

solvedExamples.title: Balance
solvedExamples.question: Critics say a policy raises prices; supporters say it protects jobs. Which ending fits best?

steps.title: Balance
steps.explanation: The paragraph has not taken a side.

solvedExamples.finalAnswer: Both claims may be partly true, so the answer depends on how the policy is designed

solvedExamples.title: Tone
solvedExamples.question: A letter says "I regret to inform you that your application has not been successful." Which ending fits?
solvedExamples.finalAnswer: We thank you for your interest and wish you every success in the future
solvedExamples.whyItWorks: A casual or boastful ending clashes.

traditionalVsShortcut.traditionalMethod: Pick the sentence that sounds good.
traditionalVsShortcut.shortcutMethod: Decide direction and tone first, then discard options that leave the topic, repeat, or leap to extremes.

commonMistakes.howToAvoid: Look for new content that closes.

placementTips.questionSelectionAdvice: Read the paragraph in your head with each option in turn.

selfCheckQuestions: Can I name direction and tone?
Can I balance a two-sided paragraph?
